weighing.summary: No source of 1863-64 gives a wind speed for 2-3 July. Both figures of the row, 12 and 2 mph, come from one printed article of 1885 (H. E. Jacobs, reporting his father's readings), which two web transcriptions read differently and which was not found. The witnesses of the time say only calm (Jacobs, morning of 2 July), little wind (Fremantle, 4.45 p. m.) and, via the Park Service, very gentle from the south-southwest (3 July). That points to a light wind but names no number, so the speed is a gap and the default is a marked range. Position C-045-P7 (the Park Service note, rank 1) outranks the stand-in only in the sense that the stand-in is no writing at all; it is not the default because it is a modern text relaying a text of 1885 and states a word and a direction for 3 July, not a speed, and the default has to supply a speed. It supports the lightness of the range and the direction of 3 July, never a figure. Direction is not settled by the record: Jacobs via Georg gives south-southwest for 3 July only, Haskell a west wind on 3 July, Toombs (1888, C-045-P9) a wind from Ewell's side (north to northeast) toward the southwest at about 4 p. m. on 2 July; nothing of the time states a direction for 2 July.
weighing.who: Jacobs, a professor at Pennsylvania College and a resident, kept the weather record that the article of 1885 reports; he is the observer behind both figures, but his 1864 book gives no speed. Fremantle, an officer attached to Longstreet's staff, wrote the diary entry on the ground. Haskell, on Gibbon's staff, wrote a letter. The Park Service historian (1981) and Toombs (1888) were not there.
weighing.when: Fremantle's diary is of the day (first printed 1863); Haskell's letter was written 'not long after the contest'; Jacobs's book is of 1864, within two years of the event; the article that carries the figures is of 1885 (22 years later); the Park Service note is of 1981. The rank of writing favours the diary and the letter, but they give no number.
weighing.where: Fremantle watched the cannonade from a tree near Longstreet; Jacobs was in the town; Haskell stood on Cemetery Ridge. A wind at one place and hour is not a wind of the whole field and day, so the words of one witness do not fix the speed of another hour.
weighing.how_knew: Jacobs kept a thermometer record; his son's article of 1885 is said (by web transcriptions, leads) to print a speed in parentheses, but how the speed was obtained (an estimate or an instrument) is not stated in anything read. Fremantle and Haskell saw smoke and a flag: impressions.
weighing.clock: not applicable: no time of the wind is in dispute; the hours given (morning of 2 July, about 4.45 p. m.) are the witnesses' own and the 20-minute difference of the two armies' clocks does not matter to a wind.
weighing.independence: Fremantle and Jacobs (1864) are independent witnesses of the light wind of 2 July; the two web transcriptions of the 1885 article, and the image of the clipping they were typed from, are one source that was read two ways (leads, not cited). The Park Service note and the project's weather record both rest on the same article of 1885. 12 mph has no non-lead source at all; nor has 2 mph.

source_panel_text: No source of the time gives a wind speed for 2-3 July. Jacobs (1864) calls the air calm on the morning of 2 July, Fremantle's diary has little wind that afternoon, and the Park Service reports Jacobs's record as very gentle. Both figures, 2 and 12 mph, appear to come from one 1885 article, not found, so a light wind of 2 to 6 mph is drawn. Nine other values stay listed.
